fullPassage: Do you think you would be happy being a child prodigy, someone who is truly gifted in something at a very young age? Maybe you would, and maybe you wouldn't. However, we live in a society that generally accepts the idea that giftedness leads to success, and success guarantees a life full of happiness. Does giftedness guarantee future success? There are two ways to answer this question. One is simply to track the achievements of precocious kids. There is a mid-1980s study of adults who attended New York City's highly regarded Hunter College Elementary School, which was founded in the 1920s as a training ground for America's future intellectual elite and only admitted children with an IQ of 155 or above. Yet the fate of the Hunter College child geniuses in the study was not greatness; it was simply being okay. Thirty years down the road, the Hunter graduates were all doing pretty well and were reasonably well adjusted and happy. Most of them had good jobs and many had advanced degrees. But surprisingly, none of the Hunter graduates became CEOs of world-famous corporations, prominent politicians, well-known writers, or Nobel Prize winners; there were no people who were nationally known in their fields. They were genius kids, but they were not genius adults. A similar pattern emerged in Ontario, Canada, in the 1970s. There was an elementary school with a team of elite runners. At that time, there were 15 nationally-ranked runners who were 13 and 14 years old. According to research done ten years later, only one runner from that group became a top runner at the age of 24. In fact, the number-one runner at the age of 24 was someone known as a poor runner when he was young, Doug Consiglio. Doug was thought to be an awkward kid. When he was 14, all the other kids asked, "Why does he even bother?" Another way to look at precocity is to work backwards — to look at adult geniuses and see what they were like as kids. A number of studies have taken this approach, and they found a similar pattern. A study of 200 highly accomplished adults found that just 34 percent had been considered precocious as children. There is also a long list of historical geniuses who were quite ordinary as children; the list includes Copernicus, Rembrandt, Bach, Newton, Beethoven, Kant, and Leonardo da Vinci. None of these geniuses would have made it into Hunter College Elementary School. As you can see from these studies, precocity is a trickier subject than people may ordinarily think. The benefits of earlier mastery are often overestimated. There are many people who either started out good and went bad or started bad and ended up good. Early acquisition of skills — which is often what we mean by precocity — may be a misleading indicator of later success. When we call a child precocious, we have a very inaccurate definition of what we mean. Generally, what we mean is that a person has an unusual level of intellectual or physical ability for his or her age. Adult success has a lot to do with more than that. In our obsession with precocity, we are exaggerating the importance of being talented. Rather, deliberate practice toward a goal is much more important than natural-born ability. For example, when we say that a great musician is naturally gifted, does that tell us that he or she practices a lot, wants to practice a lot, or likes to practice a lot? People often cite Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart as a child prodigy, someone who acquired his musical skills very early. He started to compose music at the age of four. By six, he traveled around Europe giving special performances with his father, Leopold. He is, therefore, the perfect example of a precocious child. However, there are faults in the Mozart myth. First of all, the music he composed at four isn't any good. His childhood works are basically arrangements of works by other composers. Also, rather suspiciously, they were written down by his father. Leopold was the 18th-century version of a modern day parent who goes all out to make his or her child a star. Indeed Wolfgang's legendary precocity was exaggerated somewhat by his father's probable lying about his age. Young Mozart's incredible musical ability might better be attributed to practice, practice, practice. Compelled to practice three hours a day from age three on, by age six, the young Wolfgang had practiced an astonishing 3,500 hours — three times more than anybody else in his peer group. Mozart's famous precocity as a musician was not so much natural musical ability as his ability to work hard, his circumstances, and a father that pushed him to do so. A better example for what precocity really is may be the famous intellectual late-bloomer, Einstein. According to one biographer's description of the future physicist, Einstein displayed no remarkable native intelligence as a child. His success seems to have come from certain habits and personality traits — curiosity, resolve, and determination. No doubt, these traits are not particularly fascinating, but they are, perhaps, the more essential components of genius. As seen from studies of precocity, a precocious child may not become a talented adult. Furthermore, a talented adult may not have been a precocious child. Predictions from childhood about adult performance cannot be made based on relatively fixed traits such as IQ and early acquisition of skills. Instead, many of the traits that really matter in predicting adult success are variable traits like creativity, determination, and leadership. Thus, if you want to know whether a 14-year-old runner will be a good runner when he or she is 24, you must simply wait ten years to find out how truly successful he or she has become.

ch: 어린 시절의 조숙함이 성인의 성공을 예측하는 데 한계가 있다.
어린 시절 운동 능력이 성인기까지 유지된다.

questions.passage: Mozart's famous precocity as a musician was not so much natural musical ability as his ability to work hard, his circumstances, and a father that pushed him to do so. A better example for what precocity really is may be the famous intellectual late-bloomer, Einstein. According to one biographer's description of the future physicist, Einstein displayed no remarkable native intelligence as a child. His success seems to have come from certain habits and personality traits — curiosity, resolve, and determination. No doubt, these traits are not particularly fascinating, but they are, perhaps, the more essential components of genius.
questions.stem:
다음 질문에 본문에서 찾아 영어로 답하시오. (1단어)

아인슈타인의 성공이 비롯된 것으로 보이는, 호기심과 결단력 외에 또 하나의 성격 특성은?

det.korean: resolve = 의지, 결심
det.analysis: 본문: 'His success seems to have come from certain habits and personality traits — curiosity, resolve, and determination.' 호기심(curiosity)과 결단력(determination) 외의 특성은 resolve
det.tip: resolve = 굳은 결심, 의지

questions.passage: As seen from studies of precocity, a precocious child may not become a talented adult. Furthermore, a talented adult may not have been a precocious child. Predictions from childhood about adult performance cannot be made based on relatively fixed traits such as IQ and early acquisition of skills. Instead, many of the traits that really matter in predicting adult success are variable traits like creativity, determination, and leadership. Thus, if you want to know whether a 14-year-old runner will be a good runner when he or she is 24, you must simply wait ten years to find out how truly successful he or she has become.
questions.stem:
다음 질문에 본문에서 찾아 영어로 답하시오. (2단어)

성인의 성공을 예측하는 데 IQ보다 중요한 특성들은 어떤 종류의 특성인가?

det.korean: variable traits = 가변적인 특성
det.analysis: 본문: 'many of the traits that really matter in predicting adult success are variable traits like creativity, determination, and leadership.' IQ는 fixed traits, 반대로 중요한 것은 variable traits
det.tip: variable traits(가변적 특성) ↔ fixed traits(고정적 특성)

questions.passage: When we call a child precocious, we have a very inaccurate definition of what we mean. Generally, what we mean is that a person has an unusual level of intellectual or physical ability for his or her age. Adult success has a lot to do with more than that. In our obsession with precocity, we are exaggerating the importance of being talented. Rather, __________ is much more important than natural-born ability.
questions.stem:
다음 우리말에 맞도록 조건에 맞게 영어로 쓰시오. (5단어)

[목표를 향한 의도적인 연습]

[조건] a, deliberate, goal, practice, toward를 반드시 포함할 것

det.korean: deliberate practice toward a goal = 목표를 향한 의도적인 연습
det.analysis: deliberate(의도적인) + practice(연습) + toward(~을 향한) + a goal(목표). 원문: deliberate practice toward a goal is much more important
det.tip: deliberate practice = 의도적인/계획적인 연습. toward a goal = 목표를 향한

questions.passage: As seen from studies of precocity, a precocious child may not become a talented adult. Furthermore, a talented adult may not have been a precocious child. Predictions from childhood about adult performance cannot be made based on relatively fixed traits such as IQ and early acquisition of skills. Instead, many of the traits that really matter in predicting adult success are __________ like creativity, determination, and leadership.
questions.stem:
다음 우리말에 맞도록 조건에 맞게 영어로 쓰시오. (2단어)

[가변적인 특성들]

[조건] variable, traits를 반드시 포함할 것

det.korean: variable traits = 가변적인 특성들
det.analysis: 원문: 'are variable traits like creativity, determination, and leadership.' fixed traits(고정적 특성)와 대비되는 variable traits(가변적 특성)
det.tip: variable traits = 가변적 특성 (창의성, 결단력, 리더십 등)

questions.passage: A similar pattern emerged in Ontario, Canada, in the 1970s. There was an elementary school with a team of elite runners. At that time, there were 15 nationally-ranked runners who were 13 and 14 years old. According to research done ten years later, __________ at the age of 24. In fact, the number-one runner at the age of 24 was someone known as a poor runner when he was young, Doug Consiglio.
questions.stem:
다음 우리말에 맞도록 주어진 단어를 올바르게 배열하여 영어로 쓰시오. (10단어) [그 그룹에서 단 한 명의 선수만이 최고의 선수가 되었다] [보기] a, became, from, group, one, only, runner, runner, that, top

a / became / from / group / one / only / runner / runner / that / top

→ __________

overlay.blank: only one runner from that group became a top runner

det.korean: only one runner from that group became a top runner = 그 그룹에서 단 한 명의 선수만이 최고의 선수가 되었다
det.analysis: only one runner(단 한 명의 선수만이) + from that group(그 그룹에서) + became a top runner(최고의 선수가 되었다)
det.tip: only one = 단 하나만. from that group = 그 그룹에서

questions.wa: only one runner from that group became a top runner
accept: only one runner from that group became a top runner

questions.passage: Young Mozart's incredible musical ability might better be attributed to practice, practice, practice. Compelled to practice three hours a day from age three on, __________ — three times more than anybody else in his peer group. Mozart's famous precocity as a musician was not so much natural musical ability as his ability to work hard, his circumstances, and a father that pushed him to do so.
questions.stem:
다음 우리말에 맞도록 주어진 단어를 올바르게 배열하여 영어로 쓰시오. (12단어) [여섯 살이 될 무렵, 어린 볼프강은 놀라운 3,500시간을 연습했다] [보기] 3,500, age, an, astonishing, by, had, hours, practiced, six, the, Wolfgang, young

3,500 / age / an / astonishing / by / had / hours / practiced / six / the / Wolfgang / young

→ __________

overlay.blank: by age six, the young Wolfgang had practiced an astonishing 3,500 hours

det.korean: by age six, the young Wolfgang had practiced an astonishing 3,500 hours = 여섯 살이 될 무렵, 어린 볼프강은 놀라운 3,500시간을 연습했다
det.analysis: by age six(여섯 살 무렵) + the young Wolfgang(어린 볼프강은) + had practiced(연습해왔다, 과거완료) + an astonishing 3,500 hours(놀라운 3,500시간)
det.tip: by + 시점 = ~까지/~무렵. had practiced = 과거완료(경험/완료)

questions.wa: by age six, the young Wolfgang had practiced an astonishing 3,500 hours
accept: by age six the young Wolfgang had practiced an astonishing 3,500 hours

questions.stem:
